summary.title: An algorithm for stress and mixed control in Galerkin based FFT homogenization
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces a novel algorithm for imposing macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient histories within non-linear Galerkin-based Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) homogenization. Traditional FFT methods typically enforce strain control, requiring iterative corrections to achieve stress control, which increases computational cost. The proposed method modifies the projection operator in the Fourier space, specifically at the null frequency, to directly enforce the target stress components without altering the null frequencies for strain-controlled components. This modification allows the algorithm to solve the equilibrium problem exactly as the original variational method, avoiding additional iterations in both the linear iterative solver and the Newton scheme. The authors demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of this approach through numerical examples involving a particle-reinforced hyperelastic composite and a polycrystalline material with crystal plasticity. Results show that the new method achieves the same convergence rates and simulation times as standard strain control, making it a robust tool for simulating complex loading paths like uniaxial tension or cyclic stress control without the computational penalty associated with previous stress-control techniques.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces a novel algorithm for imposing macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient histories within non-linear Galerkin-based Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) homogenization. Traditional FFT methods typically enforce strain control, requiring iterative corrections to achieve stress control, which increases computational cost. The proposed method modifies the projection operator in the Fourier space, specifically at the null frequency, to directly enforce the target stress components without altering the null frequencies for strain-controlled components. This modification allows the algorithm to solve the equilibrium problem exactly as the original variational method, avoiding additional iterations in both the linear iterative solver and the Newton scheme. The authors demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of this approach through numerical examples involving a particle-reinforced hyperelastic composite and a polycrystalline material with crystal plasticity. Results show that the new method achieves the same convergence rates and simulation times as standard strain control, making it a robust tool for simulating complex loading paths like uniaxial tension or cyclic stress control without the computational penalty associated with previous stress-control techniques.

Research Context
Computational homogenization simulates material response via RVE boundary problems. FFT methods replace differential operators with Fourier space counterparts. Imposing macroscopic stress is not a direct task in standard FFT. Standard schemes require iterative correction of applied strain to match stress. These iterative corrections significantly increase the number of iterations per step. Previous stress control methods still require a reference medium. Galerkin approaches avoid reference media but originally used strain control.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can stress and mixed control be imposed without extra iterations? Does modifying the projection operator enable direct stress enforcement? Will the new method preserve the efficiency of the original strain control scheme? Can the method handle non-linear constitutive equations like crystal plasticity? Will mixed control accurately simulate uniaxial tension without spurious stresses?

Methodological Details
The RVE is discretized in a 3D voxel grid. Linear momentum balance is imposed in its weak form. Test functions are virtual deformation gradients premultiplied by a projector. The discrete form is a convolution computed via Fourier transforms. The unknown is the deformation gradient decomposed into average and fluctuation. In strain control, the average deformation gradient is given as input. The projection operator enforces compatibility via Helmholtz decomposition. The operator projects fields into curl-free, divergence-free, and average parts. For null and Nyquist frequencies, the operator is a null fourth order tensor. For other frequencies, the operator uses the standard Green function form. Stress control requires eliminating the zero mean projection condition. The new operator projects fields into compatible and mean parts. At null frequency, the operator becomes the fourth order identity tensor. Mixed control imposes stress in specific directions and strain in others. The modified operator switches between identity and null based on control type.

Procedures And Architectures
The non-linear system is solved by splitting the macroscopic gradient into increments. A Newton scheme linearizes the stress around the last iteration. The linear system for corrections is solved using the conjugate gradient method. For rate-dependent materials, the velocity gradient is derived from time increments. The equilibrium equation for stress control includes the target stress P. The correction for deformation gradient includes a mean value under stress control. Mixed control solves for fluctuations in strain directions and full gradients in stress directions. The algorithm uses the modified operator G∗in the Newton update step. Convergence criteria use the voxel averaged L2 norm of the residual. Tolerances are 10−8 for linear solvers and 10−6 for Newton solvers.

Key Results
Hyperelastic composite: 4 particles occupy a volume fraction of 0.2. Domain discretized using 643 voxels for the hyperelastic test. Matrix shear modulus is 28 Pa and bulk modulus is 46.67 Pa. Particles are one order of magnitude stiffer than the matrix. Test reaches an elongation of λend = 0.2 in the loading direction. Load is homogeneously divided in 100 load increments. Case 1: Mixed control imposes deformation gradient in x direction. Case 2: Full stress control applies a linear ramp from 0 to target stress. Case 3: Full strain control imposes deformation gradient using a linear ramp. Cases 1 and 2 share the same path due to path independence. Case 3 develops small compressive transverse stresses due to path dependence. Polycrystal RVE contains around 200 randomly oriented grains. Final elongation of 0.02 is imposed in 200s for the polycrystal. Strain rate for polycrystal test is 5 10−5. Time is discretized in 20 regular increments for the polycrystal. Case 4 uses pseudo-uniaxial tension with full strain control. Cases 1 and 2 are not superposed due to strain rate effects. Case 4 develops non-zero compressive transverse stresses. Hyperelastic simulations needed almost identical times for every boundary condition. Polycrystal case 2 is faster due to fast elastic steps compensating plastic steps. Stress and mixed controlled simulations took approximately the same number of iterations.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The modified operator enforces stress directly without iterative correction. The method solves the problem exactly as the original variational method. No additional iterations are required in the linear or Newton schemes. The approach preserves the computational performance of the original method. Mixed control allows accurate simulation of uniaxial tension without spurious stresses. The method is applicable to any material model including crystal plasticity. The algorithm represents a useful tool for FFT based computational homogenization. It allows solving problems with mixed boundary conditions without extra computational effort.

Contradictions And Limitations
Case 3 (strain control) develops compressive transverse stresses unlike stress control. Pseudo-uniaxial tests with strain control lead to inaccurate results for polycrystals. Differences in strain rate affect the superposition of stress paths in visco-plastic materials. The fixed time step assumption may affect performance comparisons. Adaptive time stepping would likely equalize simulation times across all cases.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Performance was analyzed for hyperelastic and polycrystal models. Case 2 (full stress control) was faster than others in the polycrystal due to elastic dominance. Fixed time step was used, which may influence performance comparisons.

Figure 1 shows particle reinforced RVE and stress responses for three load cases. Figure 2 shows polycrystalline RVE and stress responses for four load cases. Figure 3 compares convergence iterations and simulation times for all cases.

A new algorithm imposes macroscopic stress or mixed control without extra iterations. The method preserves the computational performance of the original strain control scheme. The approach enables accurate simulation of mixed boundary conditions for complex materials.
